title: Design a distributed cache
prompt: Design an in-memory cache spread across many servers that sits in front of a database for a read-heavy service.

functional: Get, set and delete a value by key.
Keys are spread across many cache servers.
Entries may be evicted when memory runs out.
A value changed in the database does not stay stale in the cache.
non_functional: A get is served from memory, far faster than the database.
Losing a cache server does not push its whole load onto the database.
Adding or removing a server moves only a small share of the keys.
assumptions: A cache server gives 64 GB of memory to items.
1 million gets per second at peak.

estimates.label: Gets per server at peak, if evenly spread
Load moved to the database if one server's keys all miss

key_points.text: Memcached provides a simple set of operations: set, get and delete.
On a miss the cache hands the client a lease, a 64-bit token bound to the key, which the client presents when it sets the value.

Web servers send get requests over UDP to reduce latency and overhead, and send set and delete over TCP through mcrouter, because for operations that must confirm a state change TCP removes the need to add a retry mechanism to the UDP implementation.
A write does not update the cache: the web server writes to the database and then sends a delete, because deletes are idempotent.

data_model.system: Facebook memcache, Dynamo and Redis Cluster

key_points.text: Facebook distributes items across the memcached servers in a cluster through consistent hashing.
In consistent hashing a key is hashed to a position on a ring and assigned to the first node clockwise from it; a node arriving or leaving affects only its immediate neighbours.
Redis Cluster instead divides the key space into 16384 hash slots, computes a key's slot as CRC16(key) mod 16384, and assigns each master a subset of the slots.
The cache is not the authoritative source of the data and is therefore allowed to evict it.

notes.text: A web server asks memcache first; on a miss it reads the database and populates the cache. On a write it updates the database and deletes the key from the cache.
Hundreds of memcached servers are provisioned in a cluster, with items distributed by consistent hashing.
Gets go over UDP directly to memcached; sets and deletes go over TCP through mcrouter running on the same machine as the web server.
A small Gutter pool, about 1% of the memcached servers, takes requests for servers that have stopped responding.

blocks.name: Web server
blocks.note: The instance counts here are placeholders; the paper says hundreds of memcached servers per cluster.

checks.title: The Service reads through a Cache with a Database behind it
checks.miss: No Connection from a Service to a Cache carries the read path, or the Service has no Database behind it.

rationale.text: Facebook's memcache is a demand-filled look-aside cache: the web server requests a value from the cache and on a miss retrieves it from the database.

checks.title: A Cache runs on more than one server
checks.miss: No Cache has more than one instance.

rationale.text: Facebook provisions hundreds of memcached servers in a cluster and distributes items across them through consistent hashing.

checks.title: Every Cache has an eviction policy that frees memory
checks.miss: A Cache has no eviction policy, or uses noeviction.

rationale.text: The cache is not the authoritative source of the data and is therefore allowed to evict cached data; under noeviction Redis instead returns errors once memory is full.

deep_dives.prompt: One cache server dies. What stops the requests for its keys from overwhelming the database?

key_points.text: A client that gets no response assumes the server has failed and reissues the get to a Gutter pool, a small set of machines of about 1% of the cluster.
If the Gutter request misses, the client queries the database and inserts the result into Gutter, so later requests for that key are hits.
Gutter entries expire quickly, trading slightly stale data for not needing invalidations.
Rehashing the failed server's keys onto the remaining servers was rejected: a single key can account for 20% of a server's requests, so the inheriting server might overload too.

deep_dives.prompt: You add a seventeenth server. How do you avoid remapping most of the keys?

key_points.text: With consistent hashing the arrival or departure of a node only affects its immediate neighbours on the ring.
Virtual nodes, several positions on the ring per physical node, even out the data and load that plain random placement leaves non-uniform.
In Redis Cluster adding a node means moving hash slots to it from other nodes, which is done while the cluster is running.

deep_dives.prompt: A reader misses, reads the database, and is slow to set the value. Meanwhile a writer updates the database and deletes the key. How do you stop the reader's old value from sticking?

key_points.text: This is a stale set: a value set in the cache that does not reflect the latest value, caused by concurrent updates being reordered.
On the miss the cache gives the reader a lease, a 64-bit token bound to that key, which the reader must present when setting the value.
The writer's delete invalidates the token, so the cache refuses the reader's late set.
